primary_meaning: In Christian teaching, 'the Lamb' overwhelmingly refers to Jesus Christ as the sacrificial, atoning offering for sin — the 'Lamb of God' whose death takes away the sins of the world. The image fuses the Passover lamb of the Exodus, the lambs of the Levitical sacrificial system, and the suffering servant 'led like a lamb to the slaughter,' and it culminates in the exalted 'Lamb who was slain' worshiped in Revelation. Innocence, purity (being 'without blemish'), voluntary submission to death, redemptive substitution, and — in Revelation — paradoxical victory and kingship through sacrifice are the standard associated ideas.
primary_basis: 1 Corinthians 5:7 ('Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed')
1 Peter 1:18-19 ('a lamb without blemish or defect')
Revelation 7:14 ('washed... in the blood of the Lamb')
Genesis 22:7-8 ('God will provide the lamb' — Isaac/Akedah typology)

alternatives.meaning: The conquering/warrior Lamb of Revelation: some scholars argue the Lamb (arnion) in Revelation draws on Jewish apocalyptic traditions of a militant messianic ram or horned lamb (e.g., 1 Enoch's Animal Apocalypse, Testament of Joseph), so the image signifies messianic power and conquest, not only sacrifice. Mainstream interpretation typically holds the reverse — that Revelation deliberately subverts warrior expectations by making the slain Lamb the victor — but the warrior-lamb background reading is a recognized scholarly position.
basis: Revelation 5:5-6 (Lion of Judah revealed as Lamb)

alternatives.meaning: Lambs as symbols of Christ's followers/believers: vulnerable, innocent disciples entrusted to pastoral care. This is a distinct, well-recognized secondary use of lamb imagery, applied to the flock rather than to Christ.
basis: Luke 10:3 ('I am sending you out like lambs among wolves')

alternatives.meaning: 'Lamb of God' as the suffering-servant figure primarily, i.e., a servant/martyr identification rather than a cultic-sacrificial one; some historical-critical scholars (following e.g. C.H. Dodd and debates over the Aramaic talya, which can mean 'servant/boy' as well as 'lamb') argue John the Baptist's phrase originally denoted the Servant of the Lord or even an apocalyptic deliverer rather than a sacrificial victim.
basis: John 1:29-34 (exegetical debate over the Baptist's intent)

alternatives.meaning: The counterfeit lamb: the second beast of Revelation has 'two horns like a lamb' and is standardly read as a parody or imitation of the true Lamb (the false prophet/antichrist figure). This is a different referent, not a different reading of Christ-as-Lamb.
The daily Tamid offering as the primary background (rather than Passover): a scholarly reading that the morning-and-evening lamb of the continual burnt offering underlies 'Lamb of God' imagery.

notes: This is one of the most stable and widely attested symbols in Christian interpretation, affirmed across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions (e.g., the liturgical 'Agnus Dei') and across academic biblical scholarship. Disagreements concern which Old Testament background is primary (Passover lamb, Isaiah 53 servant, Tamid, Akedah) and how much Revelation's Lamb subverts versus embodies militant messianism — not whether the Lamb symbolizes Christ and his redemptive death. The secondary use of lamb imagery for believers is universally recognized but treated as distinct from the christological title.
